stories.headline: Assam: Jamiat, Anfar Foundation announce Rs 3.60 crore housing aid for 4,500 flood-hit families
stories.title: Assam: Jamiat, Anfar Foundation announce Rs 3.60 crore housing aid for 4,500 flood-hit families
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
article_sentences: NAZIRA: In a major humanitarian initiative, the Jamiat Ulema-e-Hind and Anfar Foundation announced financial assistance of Rs 3.60 crore for the reconstruction of houses belonging to flood-affected families in Upper Assam at a public meeting held at M.C. Club, Nazira, on November 5.

Addressing a gathering of more than 500 people, Maulana Mustaq Anfar, president of Assam State Jamiat and chief patron of Anfar Foundation, assured the people that he and his organisation would continue to stand by the people of Upper Assam in times of distress.

The relief initiative was undertaken under the leadership of Maulana Syed Arshad Madani, president of All India Jamiat Ulema-e-Hind, along with Maulana Mustaq Anfar and his associates, following the devastating floods that hit Upper Assam from July 19.

It may be recalled that on August 12, Maulana Mustaq Anfar, accompanied by office-bearers of Assam State Jamiat and Anfar Foundation, visited the flood-affected areas and interacted with victims at M.C. Club, Nazira, to assess the extent of the devastation.
During the visit, Maulana Anfar emphasised that supporting families who had lost almost everything was a humanitarian responsibility.
He appealed to people to extend help to the affected families, irrespective of caste, creed or religion.
On that occasion, Maulana Syed Arshad Madani announced a contribution of Rs 1 crore, while Assam State Jamiat and Anfar Foundation jointly pledged Rs 1.25 crore for flood relief.
Earlier, from July 29, the two organisations had distributed food supplies worth approximately Rs 30 lakh among flood victims in different parts of Upper Assam.

At the November 5 meeting, Maulana Mustaq Anfar announced that Rs 3.60 crore would be provided to approximately 4,500 flood-affected families in Upper Assam to help them reconstruct their damaged houses.
He said the distribution of assistance had already commenced.
He also announced a contribution of Rs 20 lakh to the Chief Minister's Relief Fund.
The meeting was presided over by noted social worker and advocate Mahendra Bhuyan.

stories.headline: Trump says his immigration policy 'too tough' after midterm drubbing
stories.title: Trump says his immigration policy 'too tough' after midterm drubbing
stories.summary: Washington, Nov 09: US President Donald Trump acknowledged that his immigration policy was “too tough” after a severe drubbing in the midterm elections and said he was ready to work with the Democratic Party in the years ahead. Democrats won control of both the House of Representatives and the Senate in the November 3 midterm elections, flipping several Republican-held seats in a sweeping setback for Trump. The results reflected voter dissatisfaction with his handling of the immigration issue, the economy, the Iran war and rising living costs. “I think it was too tough. I think it might be too tough,” Trump told CBS' 60 Minutes in response to a question on his administration's deportation policy. The interview was recorded on Friday and telecast on Sunday evening. Soon after the interview was recorded, Trump appointed Stephen Miller, known for his strong views against immigration, as his Chief of Staff, raising questions about whether the president would significantly soften his approach. Indian tech workers were among those worst affected by the hard-line immigration policies pursued by the Trump administration. Asked about the reasons for Republicans' resounding defeat, Trump echoed the conventional wisdom that it was due to the Iran war and gas prices, while also pointing to hostility towards Israel as a factor. “They didn’t like the war,” Trump said. “They didn’t like the fact that gasoline went up because I had it down at a low. And there’s a great dislike, incredibly, for Israel.” The president said his immigration crackdown had "both helped and hurt" him at the polls. Trump said he believed he "got an A+ for closing up the border" and "very high marks for getting the bad ones out". "But I get hurt because we also took people that had good jobs, that created one violation, or breaking of the law, and that was that they came into the country illegally," he said. "Now, there is a large part of the country that thinks that they should be put out. And there's a large part of the country that thinks that they should be allowed to stay if they're good people working in a landscaping company, or working in a hotel, or doing something, right? And in some cases, paying taxes. "I think it was too tough," the Republican leader reiterated. Trump also repeated his claim that he had prevented a nuclear war between India and Pakistan. “I've settled eight wars. I settled eight wars. I mean, India-Pakistan would've been a nuclear war. I got it settled before it got going. “They had 11 planes shot down. They were ready to go. The prime minister of Pakistan said, 'Trump saved 30-50 million lives.' I settled a lot of wars,” he said. India launched Operation Sindoor on May 7, 2025, targeting terrorist infrastructure in Pakistan and Pakistan-occupied Kashmir (PoK) following the April 22 terror attack in Pahalgam that claimed 26 lives. New Delhi has consistently rejected Trump's claims of US mediation, maintaining that the understanding to cease military action was worked out directly between the two countries' Directors General of Military Operations on May 10, 2025. India has also said that no trade-related discussions took place with the US during the conflict. Asked what he thought would happen after his death, Trump said, “I hope I'm missed.” He also described himself as a “religious person” and said he hoped to go to heaven.

stories.headline: Defence Minister celebrates Diwali with soldiers in forward areas of Sikkim
stories.title: Defence Minister celebrates Diwali with soldiers in forward areas of Sikkim
stories.summary: New Delhi, Nov 8: Defence Minister Rajnath Singh on Sunday celebrated Diwali with soldiers of the Trishakti Corps (33 Corps) deployed in the forward areas of Sikkim, praising their dedication and vigilance in safeguarding the country's borders under challenging high-altitude conditions. Accompanied by Chief of the Army Staff General Dhiraj Seth, Eastern Army Commander Lt Gen VMB Krishnan and General Officer Commanding, 33 Corps, Lt Gen Man Raj Singh Mann, the Defence Minister interacted with troops at Sherathang on November 8. Describing the soldiers as the “brightest lights of Diwali”, Rajnath Singh said their commitment to duty at the borders gave the entire nation a sense of security. “Like a lamp which dispels darkness without seeking attention, soldiers perform their duties silently, ensuring that citizens can celebrate festivals with peace and security,” he said. The Defence Minister commended the troops for their professionalism, high morale and commitment to protecting the country's borders. He also acknowledged the sacrifices of soldiers who remain away from their families during festivals, placing national duty above personal celebrations. Emphasising the importance of discipline and courage, he said that even the most advanced technology would be of little use if a soldier lacked these qualities. He also stressed that the conduct, uniform, language and restraint of Army personnel shaped the image of the military among local communities. He urged the soldiers to strengthen the bond of trust and goodwill between the Army and people in Sherathang and surrounding areas. During the visit, Rajnath Singh paid homage to soldiers who laid down their lives in the service of the nation at the Sherathang War Memorial. He also visited the Baba Harbhajan Singh Memorial and paid respects to the revered soldier. Highlighting the importance of war memorials, he said they did more than commemorate past sacrifices as they helped shape collective memory and strengthen national consciousness and pride. He pointed out that the soldiers remembered at the Sherathang memorial belonged to different parts of the country, including Nagaland, Uttar Pradesh, Tamil Nadu, Rajasthan and Assam, but had made the supreme sacrifice to protect people irrespective of their region, language or community. “This spirit of unity and selfless service is the very soul and ethos of India, where every citizen considers fellow Indians as members of one family,” he said. The Defence Minister also referred to the National War Memorial in New Delhi, established by the government under the leadership of Prime Minister Narendra Modi to honour soldiers who made the supreme sacrifice. He said approximately 26,000 names of fallen soldiers had been inscribed in golden letters at the memorial, adding that these names evoked a deep sense of pride among their families and people from their native villages and regions. He said such memorials served as a source of inspiration for present and future generations.

stories.headline: Trump Era: Beginning of the End
stories.title: Trump Era: Beginning of the End
stories.summary: As the counting of votes for the American midterm elections was only almost over, it was clear that the Democratic Party won both the House of Representatives and the Senate by a huge margin. This big victory brings a major shift in the power corridors of Washington and marks the beginning of the end of the Trump era. Donald Trump has been a great disruption to the liberal world order that had guided international relations for several decades. That world order was built after terrible conflicts to ensure peace, open discussion, and mutual respect among democratic countries. Instead of strengthening friendly ties and working with age old partners, his administration treated global diplomacy like a private business deal. Every international agreement was questioned, long standing friendships were strained, and democratic institutions faced constant pressure. The American public has now given a firm and mature verdict against this disruptive style of governance. By placing both houses of Congress in the hands of the opposition, the voters have put a strong check on absolute presidential power. Common citizens across the United States have grown tired of continuous political drama, sudden midnight announcements on social media, and social division. This election demonstrates that the people genuinely want calm administration, democratic decency, and respect for established rules rather than daily noise and political arrogance. The sphere of global commerce suffered very badly during these past few years because of his erratic decisions. His trade policies were completely unpredictable and brought immense headaches to businesses across the globe. One day steep duties were imposed on goods from partner countries, and the very next day angry warnings were issued against friendly nations. In doing so, he delivered a very serious blow to the well established Washington consensus. For decades, this consensus had encouraged open markets, reduction of custom tariffs, and smooth commercial exchange through bodies like the World Trade Organization. By launching bitter trade disputes and adopting narrow protectionist attitudes, his administration harmed international supply chains, increased expenses for everyday consumers, and created severe difficulties for developing economies like India. Along with this chaotic approach to commerce, his immigration policies will hurt America as well. The United States grew into a global superpower mainly because it opened its doors to bright minds and dedicated workers from all over the world. Thousands of skilled Indian techies, doctors, scientists, and researchers have spent decades building American software empires, healthcare networks, and academic centers. By creating endless troubles for work visas, bringing hostile rules, and treating immigrants with needless suspicion, his policies have driven away top talent. Instead of strengthening national security, this narrow vision has harmed the creative spark and economic future of America itself. In the field of global diplomacy, his foreign policy has been nothing short of a total disaster. There was no coherent strategy, no consultation with career diplomats, and no calm calculation of ground realities. As the foreign affairs analyst Fareed Zakaria correctly observed, Donald Trump took the country dangerously close to an Iran war without any clear goals, sensible thinking, or realistic exit strategies. Foreign policy cannot be run like a reality television show where sudden impulses dictate national security decisions. Such dangerous actions created severe panic across West Asia and badly damaged the trust of international allies who look up to Washington for steady leadership. His disregard for multilateralism made matters worse. By sidelining the United Nations, cutting support for global institutions, and preferring one-on-one bargains with weaker nations over collective decision making, he weakened the very forums where shared problems are meant to be solved. Multilateralism has long been the only real voice that small and middle powers have in world affairs, and undermining it left them more exposed to the will of the strong. Along with this diplomatic adventurism, his environmental policies have been a tragic setback to the hard won commitments and collective progress achieved since the early 1990s. International summits and environmental leaders had spent thirty years building landmark treaties like the Kyoto Protocol and the Paris Climate Agreement to protect our earth. Donald Trump simply walked away from these crucial pacts, dismissed sound environmental science, and weakened essential pollution controls. At a time when countries of the Global South, who contributed least to global emissions, bear the heaviest burden of erratic rainfall, rising seas, and deadly heat waves, and are still waiting for the climate finance and technology promised to them, turning a blind eye to climate change was an act of complete irresponsibility. The clear message from this midterm election reaches far beyond the borders of America, and indeed the world must heave a sigh of relief. Today our world faces massive global challenges such as rising temperatures, economic uncertainty, and regional unrest, which no single country can resolve on its own. We cannot afford a superpower that acts in a reckless manner and plays politics with planetary safety. The world deserves a better political hegemon that will work sincerely to make the entire planet more safe and secure for everyone. A genuine global leader ought to behave like a mature and responsible guardian who respects global agreements, supports fair commerce, and cooperates with all nations big and small. The loss of both legislative chambers shows that the American public has chosen to return to common sense, stability, and institutional balance. It will certainly take many years of hard work to heal old diplomatic wounds and restore trust in global treaties, but this electoral result gives genuine hope to peace loving people across the globe. Dr Sajad Padder, an academic based in Kashmir, teaches Political Science in Higher Education.

stories.headline: From Jesus & Mary College student to the Chief Justice's chair: Who is Justice B V Nagarathna, set for a 37-day CJI stint?
stories.title: From Jesus & Mary College student to the Chief Justice's chair: Who is Justice B V Nagarathna, set for a 37-day CJI stint?
stories.summary: Justice Nagarathna was appointed an Additional Judge of the Karnataka High Court on February 18, 2008.
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
event term: 'chief justice' in title weight 42
article_sentences: Justice B V Nagarathna was born on October 30, 1962, in Bengaluru.
She is the daughter of former Chief Justice of India E S Venkataramiah, who served as the 19th CJI in 1989, as per her profile shared by SCC.
She studied history at Jesus and Mary College, Delhi University, and graduated in 1984.
She later completed her law degree from the Campus Law Centre, Delhi University, in 1987.
After enrolling as an advocate in 1987, she practised law in Bengaluru.
Her practice covered constitutional, administrative, commercial and family law, among other areas.
Justice Nagarathna was appointed an Additional Judge of the Karnataka High Court on February 18, 2008.
She became a permanent judge on February 17, 2010.
During her years at the Karnataka High Court, she handled cases across several areas of law and also took on judicial and administrative responsibilities.
She was elevated to the Supreme Court in August 2021 and took oath as a judge on August 31 that year.
Justice Nagarathna has been part of several important Constitution Bench matters at the Supreme Court.
Her separate opinions in some of these cases have received considerable attention.

stories.headline: Deepavali 2026: All you need to know about Supreme Court-permitted time slots, green crackers and other directives
stories.title: Deepavali 2026: All you need to know about Supreme Court-permitted time slots, green crackers and other directives
stories.summary: The Supreme Court permitted the bursting of certified green firecrackers between 6 a.m. and 7 a.m. and between 8 p.m. and 10 p.m. on November 7 and November 8, 2026 in Delhi-NCR

article_sentences: The Supreme Court on November 2, 2026 described bursting of firecrackers during Deepavali as a “religious practice” while permitting the use of green firecrackers for two days, on November 7 and November 8, in Delhi-NCR.

The unregulated use of firecrackers during Deepavali has historically led to a sharp rise in the Air Quality Index (AQI) and pollution levels, including the emission of particulate matter, the court observed.

“The right of an individual to engage in a particular practice, which may have a religious colour, is only a qualified one and cannot go beyond the Constitutional restrictions,” the Supreme Court held.
The state had “utterly failed” to comply with the Supreme Court’s orders issued since 2015 to impose restrictions on fireworks, the Bench said.

stories.headline: Supreme Court Directs Rajasthan To Frame Policy For Financial Assistance To Industries Setting Up Zero Liquid Discharge Plants
stories.title: Supreme Court Directs Rajasthan To Frame Policy For Financial Assistance To Industries Setting Up Zero Liquid Discharge Plants
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
event term: 'supreme court' in title weight 44
article_sentences: The Supreme Court has directed the Rajasthan government to formulate a comprehensive policy for extending financial assistance to industrial units seeking to establish Zero Liquid Discharge (ZLD) plants.
The Court directed the state to consider applications for such assistance on a case-to-case basis pending formulation of the policy.

A bench of Justice Vikram Nath and Justice Sandeep Mehta passed the order in the suo motu proceedings concerning pollution in the Jojari-Luni-Bandi river system, which has affected the environment and the lives of approximately 20 lakh people.
“The State of Rajasthan shall formulate a comprehensive policy for extending financial assistance to industrial units desirous of establishing ZLD plants.

Pending formulation of such policy, the State shall duly consider applications seeking financial assistance for the establishment of ZLD plants and the associated pipeline network on a case-to-case basis, upon due technical appraisal and verification, and take an appropriate decision expeditiously”, the Court ordered.

The Court directed the State to consider applications seeking financial assistance for establishing ZLD plants and associated pipeline networks upon technical appraisal and verification, and take appropriate decisions expeditiously.

It further directed Rajasthan to establish an appropriate redistribution pipeline network for conveying and reusing treated wastewater and RO permeate, facilitating optimum utilisation by industrial units and minimising the discharge of effluents into the river systems.
The State has to examine the technical and financial requirements for establishing such a network and prepare a time-bound implementation plan.

“The State of Rajasthan shall take necessary steps to establish an appropriate redistribution pipeline network for the conveyance and reuse of treated wastewater and RO permeate, so as to facilitate its optimum utilisation by industrial units and minimise the discharge of effluents into the river systems.
The State shall examine the technical and financial requirements for establishing such a network and prepare a time-bound plan for its implementation”, the Cour directed.

The Court passed the directions due to concerns raised by the High-Level Ecosystem Oversight Committee over inadequate progress in establishing and augmenting Common Effluent Treatment Plants (CETPs) and ZLD facilities in the Jodhpur, Pali and Balotra industrial clusters.
The Committee observed that administrative assurances and projected completion dates could not substitute for treatment capacity commensurate with the volume of industrial effluent generated.
